items.body: Ashley and Joshua Durham used the Affordable Care Act marketplace for their health insurance after they began their family medicine practice in Boise, Idaho, in late 2023. But the couple say they opted out of health insurance for their family of four this year after they saw their ACA premium payments jump to nearly $1,600 a month. (Photo by Hayat Norimine/KFF Health News) This story was first published by KFF Health News on Sept. 22, 2026. Joshua and Ashley Durham run a family medicine practice, and for the first time in their lives, they have no health insurance. When the Durhams began their practice at the end of 2023 — he as a primary care physician and she as a pharmacist who handles the billing — the couple bought coverage for themselves and their two kids on the Affordable Care Act marketplace. But they said their monthly premiums for a similar health plan for this year rose several hundred dollars to nearly $1,600. Top insurance official recommends task force for studying Idaho’s most critical healthcare issues They decided to pay out-of-pocket for their medical expenses instead, leaning on $50,000 they had set aside in a health savings account over several years. “It’s nerve-racking,” said Joshua Durham, 47. “It just takes, you know, one little accident, and then you got a big fat bill.” The healthcare industry traditionally has more of its workforce on medical insurance than many other fields. Nationwide, 7% of all healthcare workers were uninsured in 2024, compared with 11% of all adults under 65, according to a KFF analysis of the most recent American Community Survey data. And doctors were especially unlikely to forgo health insurance, with just 2% uninsured. But even healthcare workers are feeling the pinch as health insurance costs rise each year, with employers expecting that costs will jump an additional 8.2% for 2027. The Republican-led Congress also opted last year not to renew Affordable Care Act marketplace credits enacted during the covid pandemic. While subsidies remain in place for people with low incomes, the pandemic-era credits helped reduce many consumers’ premium payments , especially those working in small businesses such as independent medical practices. Nearly half of marketplace enrollees worked for small businesses or were self-employed in 2024; some of the most common occupations included chiropractic care and dentistry. Jack Dillon, executive director of the Association for Independent Medicine , which represents 4,000 physician-led practices, said premium increases have become untenable for small businesses, whether employers seek coverage through the marketplace or directly from insurers. “The cost has become so astronomical,” Dillon said. “You’re looking at it and saying, ‘What’s the value?’” As health insurance continues to become less affordable, Dillon said, more healthcare employers may seek alternatives to their standard coverage, such as providing higher hourly wages or providing only minimal plans. The number of people without insurance in the U.S. is expected to increase by roughly 15 million over 10 years because of the expiration of the expanded ACA subsidies and $1.1 trillion in estimated cuts resulting from President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to the Congressional Budget Office. Healthier people are the most likely to opt out of insurance. That leaves insurance covering a smaller pool of people who tend to be sicker and need more expensive care. So insurers raise prices to cover the remaining enrollees, which fuels even higher premium costs. YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. items.body: School funding was central to both candidates’ pitches at Tuesday’s state superintendent debate at the College of Idaho. Republican incumbent Debbie Critchfield touted her efforts this spring and summer to rewrite the state’s more than 30-year-old funding formula, her top priority if re-elected. She pointed to her relationships with legislators as key to helping pass a fund for high-needs students last legislative session, along with other education priorities. Those relationships, she said, will help her push a funding formula rewrite across the finish line next session if reelected. Democratic challenger Becky Sundin Mitchell emphasized enrollment-based funding and questioned whether Critchfield could succeed where previous state superintendents have failed: getting lawmakers to approve a new K-12 funding formula. Sundin Mitchell stressed that Idaho’s public schools need more funds, in general, as they routinely rank 51st in the nation for per-pupil spending . She repeatedly called for legislators to spend more time in public schools. The debate, hosted by Idaho Education News and The College of Idaho, provided a glimpse into the candidates’ different approaches to school funding and a range of other issues, including the role of the state superintendent, a lingering special education funding gap, Idaho’s new private school tax credit, and how much politics should shape education policy. A livestream of the debate is available on EdNews’ Facebook page . items.body: The Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals as photographed on June 12, 2017, in San Francisco, California. A panel of Ninth Circuit judges heard arguments Tuesday in a lawsuit challenging Idaho's abortion ban, seeking expanded exemptions. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) A panel of federal appeals judges will soon decide whether to continue to allow full enforcement of Idaho’s abortion bans, or to allow a lower court’s previous ruling that provided more exemptions to the law. U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit Judges Kim McLane Wardlaw, Marsha Berzon and Consuelo Callahan heard oral arguments in a virtual hearing Tuesday afternoon. The state of Idaho, represented by an attorney from the conservative Christian legal advocacy group Alliance Defending Freedom , argued that the laws should be fully enforced as written. Idaho’s laws prohibit most abortions, except in cases to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors face felony penalties and civil lawsuits of a minimum of $20,000 if they perform the procedure outside those exemptions. ADF attorney Mathew Hoffmann argued that a lower court’s previous ruling that would’ve expanded exemptions to apply to serious health and mental health risks to the mother, was not grounded in historical precedent. He said there is no right to “therapeutic” abortions. Attorneys representing Boise maternal-fetal medicine specialist Dr. Stacy Seyb argued that an earlier court decision from U.S. District of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill should go back into effect. The ruling would’ve prevented the Ada County prosecutor and Idaho attorney general from enforcing Idaho’s abortion ban in cases where the mother’s health faced serious risk or her life was at risk due to self harm. Winmill later narrowed this block on enforcement to only protect abortions performed by Seyb. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador. (Photo courtesy of Attorney General Raúl Labrador) After Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed, a Ninth Circuit panel placed a hold on Winmill’s order, and the law went back into effect. Hoffmann said Winmill’s decision expanding the exemptions created “an abortion-on-demand regime.” “They leave it up to the subjective judgment of doctors to determine a risk sufficient to justify abortion,” he said. Stephanie Toti, executive director of the Lawyering Project, argued on behalf of Seyb that the expanded exemptions to the law were necessary. “The injunction entered by the district court in this case is narrow. It would enable only a small number of patients each year to obtain an abortion,” Toti said. “But for those patients, access to that care is vitally important, as the district court found.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Judges’ question Dobbs interpretation, abortion rights initiative, legal guidance Judges questioned the attorneys on whether the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2022 Dobbs decision, which overturned Roe v. Wade and sent regulation of abortion to the states, would allow a court to expand a state’s exemptions. Hoffmann argued that it would not, because the Constitution does not explicitly provide a right to abortions. Toti argued that the 2022 decision did not mention rights to life and health, which she said are violated by the Idaho ban’s limited exemptions. Callahan questioned Toti over whether the request to allow abortions for serious risk of self harm was “weaker” than the other arguments. “We have a right to life, but you don’t have a right to kill yourself, right?” Callahan asked. Toti responded that patients seeking an abortion to prevent death by self-harm, “don’t want to kill themselves.” “They want to remain alive. items.summary: The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State's Office, the University of Idaho's College of Law and Boise State University's Institute for Advancing American Values. (Photo by Getty Images) A new gathering aims to bring together policymakers, students and the public to discuss the U.S. Constitution’s protections for fr
items.body: The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State's Office, the University of Idaho's College of Law and Boise State University's Institute for Advancing American Values. (Photo by Getty Images) A new gathering aims to bring together policymakers, students and the public to discuss the U.S. Constitution’s protections for free speech and encourage civil discourse. The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State’s Office, the University of Idaho’s College of Law and Boise State University’s Institute for Advancing American Values , according to a Secretary of State’s Office press release. The keynote speaker for the event will be Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, who has championed Disagree Better, a national, nonpartisan initiative “designed to reduce inflammatory rhetoric and foster a culture of healthy debate,” according to its website. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane. (Photo courtesy of Phil McGrane) “Free speech is fundamental to our system of government, but protecting it requires more than simply agreeing that it is important,” said Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane. “It means listening to people we disagree with, defending their right to speak, and being willing to have difficult conversations. That is what we hope to accomplish with the Idaho Free Speech Summit.” Sessions at the summit will explore First Amendment issues “ranging from campaign finance and campus free speech to the broader challenges of maintaining civil discourse in an increasingly divided political environment,” the press release said. Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson (left) listens as Gov. Spencer Cox holds a press conference to present his budget proposal at the Salt Lake County Library in Kearns, Utah, on Dec. 3, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) Cox will talk about how Americans can disagree without abandoning strongly held beliefs, a theme he explores in his new book, “Off Ramp: How to Be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt,” according to the release. “We are pleased to be part of a discussion centered on one of our nation’s most important constitutional freedoms,” said Brian Kane, University of Idaho College of Law dean, in the release. “The University of Idaho College of Law is a natural partner for this conversation. Law schools should be places where difficult constitutional questions are examined carefully and where people learn how to engage seriously with ideas they may not share.” The daylong summit will have presentations and panel discussions, followed by an evening reception. A continuing legal education credit will also be available for participating attorneys. “Universities have an important role to play in creating spaces where people can wrestle with difficult questions and hear perspectives different from their own,” said Boise State University’s Andrew Finstuen in the release. “The Summit provides an opportunity to model the kind of thoughtful, constructive dialogue that is essential to a healthy civic culture.” Registration and additional information, including the Summit schedule and speaker lineup, are available at FreeSpeechIdaho.com . “Our goal isn’t to bring together people who all agree,” McGrane said in the release. “It is to bring together people who recognize that our constitutional freedoms are strongest when we defend the right of others to speak, listen to one another, and engage in good faith.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. Dame Nursing and Allied Health Professions Center will house the college’s new Registered Nurse to Bachelor of Science in Nursing degree program, which will launch Sept. 28 with a cohort of five students. items.body: A $7.9 million lab expansion is slated to begin this fall at Idaho State University’s Meridian campus — a project geared to support two partners seeking to address Idaho’s physician shortage. The project will add a 16-station human anatomy lab and a two-station embalming suite at the L.S. and Aline W. Skaggs Treasure Valley Anatomy and Physiology Laboratories. The building is home to a 34-station anatomy lab, Idaho State said in a news release. But demand is increasing, and the 6,130-square-foot remodel is designed to keep up with future growth. “We have a decade of very successful operations under our belt,” said Padma Gadepally, director of anatomy laboratories and clinical assistant professor at Idaho State. “We started with about 50 learners and now have upwards of 2,000 learners.” Existing lab space at the L.S. and Aline W. items.body: Sal Soto struggled through high school, making it to graduation with the help of summer classes. He never thought decades later he’d be back at high school every day as a teacher, helping students like himself. Soto, 44, is the culinary teacher at Elevate Academy Nampa, one of a handful of career technical education charter schools in the Elevate network statewide. At Elevate, he has turned his experience as a restaurant owner into more than a culinary program. His classroom is built around relationships, hands-on learning, and the idea that students can learn from their mistakes — lessons Soto says he learned the hard way. Learning the family business Soto was born and raised in Caldwell. His parents immigrated from Mexico and worked their way up at major Idaho agribusiness company JR Simplot Co. When he was 12, the Sotos took a risk opening Imelda’s, a TexMex restaurant in Caldwell. His mother, Imelda, used family recipes to create the restaurant’s menu. “It was a lot of stress on them,” Soto said. “She would be like, ‘Was this a good switch’ from being a boss at Simplot to opening up her own business.” Soto would do his homework at the restaurant before helping wherever he was needed. He graduated high school and did odd jobs for a few years before being drawn back to the restaurant, which he purchased from his mother in his early 20s. His mother taught him how to cook. “I had many fails,” Soto said with a chuckle. He was nervous taking over the business and trying to prove himself to the customers. “We got really busy,” he said. “It was stressful. It was like, ‘OK this is a lot on me.'” The regular customers were the best part, Soto said. The restaurant is near the College of Idaho campus, so basketball, football and volleyball players would come frequently. It began to feel like family. items.body: Absentee ballots are prepared to be mailed at the Wake County Board of Elections on September 17, 2024 in Raleigh, North Carolina. (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images) With less than two months before the 2026 midterm elections, election officials across Idaho mailed the first round of mail-in ballots to voters who are overseas or who requested absentee ballots locally. The finalization of ballots in Idaho follows after a weekslong crunch to change contested language for an abortion legalization ballot initiative and attempts by the Trump administration to implement a federal rule that could’ve made last-minute changes to ballots. Idaho election officials worry about mail-in ballot changes proposed by Trump administration “Everything is on track,” said Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, the state’s top election official who’s running for re-election as a Republican. More than a month before the Nov. 3 general election, local election officials are expected to finalize ballots. That’s because federal law requires the first slate of mail-in ballots be shipped 45 days before federal elections to voters who are overseas, such as members of the military or missionaries. In Ada County, Idaho’s largest, election officials were expecting to mail out more than 24,000 ballots on Friday, Trent Tripple, the Republican county clerk, told the Idaho Capital Sun. That includes overseas and military voters, along with everyone who had already requested an absentee ballot, he said. Voters still have more than a month to request absentee ballots or register to vote before Election Day. Oct. 23 is the deadline to request absentee ballots or pre-register to vote, according to an election calendar on VoteIdaho.gov , a website run by the Secretary of State’s Office. This year, all statewide constitutional offices — such as governor, lieutenant governor, and attorney general — are up for election as well as all 105 seats in the Idaho Legislature. Three of Idaho’s four congressional seats will also be on the ballot. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. Idaho Secretary of State candidate Phil McGrane talks with a supporter during the Idaho Republican Party primary celebration on May 17, 2022. items.body: The Columbia Princess Ferry stays on the Gifford side of the Columbia River as the Modrite Fire exhibits extreme fire behavior just south of Inchelium, Washington. Fires in the state hit tribes particularly hard this year. (Photo courtesy of Colville Tribal Broadcasts, News and Information) Neighbors across the Colville Tribes communities in Washington state knew Matilda Bob’s log home as the “rainbow house,” for its brightly painted exterior. Now it’s gone. Sparked by a lightning strike in mid-July, the Kaiser Canyon Fire destroyed Bob’s home and 42 other houses on the Colville Reservation, along with 100 outbuildings such as sheds and barns, tribal leaders said. “I couldn’t believe that it had happened,” said Bob. “It went so fast.” Tribal leaders across Washington and Oregon told Stateline that this year’s record-breaking wildfires burned timber that they rely on for income, threatened food sources and waterways, and harmed the health of their communities. Power outages left families without food they’ve hunted or gathered and frozen. Hotter, drier conditions driven by climate change already have made wildfires nationwide more frequent and intense, a trend that is expected to accelerate. Substandard housing and higher rates of acute and chronic underlying health conditions, including respiratory illnesses, make tribal communities more vulnerable during and after the fires. “What typically used to be like a two-month fire season for us when I first started fighting fire about 25 years ago — now that’s at least three months and sometimes longer, depending on the year,” said Cody Desautel , executive director of the Colville Tribes, who is also a forester and wildland fire expert. An especially warm winter also left Washington state with about half its usual snowpack, raising drought concerns and wildfire risks. Nighttime view of the Kaiser Canyon Fire during firing operations on Whitmore Mountain. (Photo courtesy of Colville Tribal Broadcasts, News and Information) This year saw particularly devastating fires in eastern Washington, including arson-instigated fires that destroyed over 700 homes in Spokane. The conditions prompted Washington state Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson to declare a statewide state of emergency on Aug. 1, citing an “unprecedented” red flag alert of extreme fire danger from the National Weather Service. The Colville Reservation includes the southern portion of Ferry County, which has the second-lowest median household income of all counties in the state. The tribe lost a significant amount of timber, a main source of income, during the fires. Many residents didn’t have home insurance because the housing didn’t qualify or they couldn’t afford it, said Cindy Marchand, chairwoman of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, adding that about half of homes destroyed in the fires weren’t insured. Other residents couldn’t afford to upgrade to more fire-resistant material, she said. “The rates are just astronomical in the sense that a lot of people in our area are not able to afford this,” Marchand said. “We have elders living on a single income, they’re on a fixed income, and so they’re having a hard time making it as it is.” By mid-September, the total acres burned across the state reached roughly 900,000 acres, the worst since 2015. Since July, about 200,000 acres burned across the Colville Reservation alone, with the Kaiser Canyon Fire scorching over 138,000 acres and the Modrite fire burning more than 57,000 acres. In Oregon, over 60,000 acres burned across the reservation of the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs, where at least six homes were destroyed. The Wrights Spring Fire in Oregon burned through 55,000 acres across Klamath County, national forest and tribal lands. items.body: The Kuna Lions Club is sponsoring health screening for vision, hearing and diabetes from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Oct. 10 at Kuna’s community center. (Photo by Getty Images) Here’s something that you should not pass up. The Kuna Lions (my club) is sponsoring health screening for vision, hearing and diabetes from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Oct. 10 at Kuna’s community center. The vision and hearing screening will be conducted by Envision , and Terry Reilly Health Services will be doing the diabetes testing. People living in surrounding communities are cordially invited. If there were a poster boy for diabetes screening, it would be me. This has been a summer of amputations – one toe on my right foot and two partial toe amputations on my left foot. I have not been able to do summer activities that I enjoy, such as daily walks around the neighborhood and golf. Yes, these amputations were the result of diabetes. On the bright side, losing a couple of toes is a lot better than losing a foot or a leg. But there’s more to my diabetes story. Twenty-two years ago, I had a five-way heart bypass surgery – which has given me more than two decades of quality living. But veins from that surgery don’t last forever, and some of mine have shown signs of wear. In football terms, I may be getting close to the two minute warning. But as fans know so well, a lot can happen in those last two minutes. I have a great life, and it isn’t done yet. I might have been spared from some of these health challenges if I had diabetes screening 30 years ago. Instead, I ignored some of the obvious symptoms. Recently, I had a chat with Dr. Stuart Black with Terry Reilly Health Services, and he knows all about the importance of the screening. “Some studies show that 10 percent of the population, and as high as 13 percent have diabetes and maybe a fourth of the people with diabetes don’t know about it,” he said. “If screening shows an indication of prediabetes, people can get the care they need and prevent the complications that come with the disease, such as heart disease and kidney problems. Diabetes also is one of the leading causes for blindness.” Dr. Black says that random glucose readings at a screening event may not paint the true picture. For instance, numbers may be on the high side for those who had something to eat before the screening. But high numbers are worth watching. “The more information that a person has, the better,” he says. “I think there are people who are afraid to find out they have diabetes, because they think it’s a death sentence. But that’s not the case. There are great options to help control blood sugars if you have diabetes or prediabetes.” Terry Reilly’s service doesn’t stop with the screening. It’s also a resource, and a relatively affordable one, for those who show signs of prediabetes or diabetes. Terry Reilly Health Services, based in Nampa, has other area clinics – including one in Melba. “We have physicians and clinical pharmacists who are well versed in dealing with diabetes,” Dr. Black said. “Our doors are open to help anyone who is diagnosed, or at risk, for diabetes or prediabetes.” Of course, he says, there are steps people can take without a doctor’s help. “Getting 150 minutes of exercise in a week; eating a healthy diet that focuses more on fruits, vegetables and less on fast foods or processed foods; getting enough sleep; decreasing stress in your life,” he said. “All those things are basic lifestyle choices that people can take, with or without diabetes.” I wish I had followed that advice 30 years ago. items.body: The Canyon County Sheriff’s Office on Friday confirmed its investigation into the Vallivue School District’s 2024 land deal is still active. Idaho EdNews broke the story on April 17. “No updates at this time, investigation still active,” a detective with the criminal investigation division told EdNews Friday. The district in 2024 bought 87 acres of farmland from Dave Christensen, the father of trustee Clay Christensen, for $5 million. The land, intended for the site of a school, was appraised at $2.87 million. “I knew about what I wanted, and, you know, it was really the only way I probably would have sold it,” Dave Christensen told EdNews in April about his $5 million price tag for the land. Idaho code requires trustees to have property appraised before a purchase and that appraisal “shall be used to establish the value of the real property.” Superintendent Lisa Boyd at the time defended the purchase and said the district complied with statute. Later that month, EdNews obtained records from several other Idaho school districts that showed Vallivue’s deal bucked the norm by millions. Five different land purchases in districts from around the state came in under the appraised value — and in two deals landowners gifted chunks of property — according to public records EdNews examined in a spot check of transactions over the past two decades. Vallivue trustees have declined to answer any questions about the land deal. Trustee Toni Brinegar, who was board chair at the time of the 2024 purchase, referred EdNews to their attorney. Two trustees have since resigned, leaving the board with three members. Brinegar resigned in June, and Paul Tierney resigned in August. Boyd said both trustees had planned to resign after their kids graduated from Vallivue schools. The district is looking for interested residents to apply for the vacancies.

Sara LaWall, the minister for the Boise Unitarian Universalist Fellowship, and eight others who were protesting bills restricting transgender rights were arrested this spring after refusing to leave the lobby to the office of Idaho Gov. Brad Little, whom the protestors said they were hoping to meet with. LaWall’s defense attorney cast her actions during the protest as an act of civil disobedience, an act that involves intentionally breaking laws for moral reasons. Brendan Gomez, 27, was arrested in early July by Ada County Sheriff’s Office detectives at a home in Boise, Channel 2 Idaho News reported. He was booked into the Ada County jail and held on $500,000 bail, according to the jail roster. He was charged with 10 counts of willfully possessing child sex abuse material, according to state court records. He entered a plea deal Monday, pleading guilty to two counts of possession of sexually exploitative materials. His sentencing hearing is scheduled for Nov. 16, according to court records. The state recommended Gomez serve a fixed term of three years in prison, with 12 years indeterminate. Gomez’s attorney could not be immediately reached for this story. Gomez also ran for Congress in 2024, earning about 1.5% of the vote in the general election. In 2022, he ran unsuccessfully against incumbent state Sen. Lori Den Hartog to represent District 22 in the Idaho Legislature. Gomez’s name will still appear on the ballot for the Nov. 3 general election. He is running against incumbent Republican U.S. House Rep. Russ Fulcher, Democrat Kaylee Peterson, and independent Sarah Zabel. The deadline to withdraw from the ballot was Sept. 4. Under the Idaho Constitution , convicted felons are ineligible for state or local office until they fulfill their sentence, but there are no such restrictions for federal elected officials. Members of the U.S. House must be at least 25 years old, a U.S. citizen for at least seven years, and an inhabitant of the state they represent.The U.S. Constitution does not otherwise limit eligibility. Under U.S. House rules , members who are convicted of a crime with a sentence of two or more years of imprisonment “should refrain” from participating in votes and “should resign” from any committee. But if graded on a curve, the Boise State and U of I grades look a little bit better. Both universities received a “D” from the Philadelphia-based Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression . Using student surveys, FIRE ranked 261 colleges and universities; 121 received failing grades. The September 2025 slaying of conservative activist Charlie Kirk had far-reaching effects, FIRE said. Some colleges denied recognition for chapters of Kirk’s Turning Point USA, while nine schools punished faculty members who publicly criticized Kirk. “The overall state of free speech on campus is grim,” FIRE President and CEO Greg Lukianoff said in a news release. “Too many college administrators wield their power to cancel controversial speakers, cave to government or student calls for censorship, and limit academic freedom.” FIRE rated only two Idaho universities. Click on the links for the full reports on Boise State and the U of I . Here are a few thumbnails. Boise State: overall ranking, 59 of 261 Boise State earned a top 50 ranking for “political tolerance,” a signal that students are willing to host controversial speakers. But the university ranked in the bottom 50 for “openness,” according to the FIRE report, “meaning many contentious topics feel off-limits to students.” Anonymous student quotes from FIRE’s survey One student reported an exchange from class: A professor said she was very upset with the outcome of the presidential election, and asked students to sum up their thoughts in one word. The student had a response in mind, contentment, but was reluctant to express it. “I thought I would get attacked or judged if I said that,” the student wrote. Another student, a lesbian, said she is often frightened to discuss her partner’s gender. “I am afraid of my fellow students.” Boise State student survey results, by the numbers 47% of students say they have self-censored, at least once or twice a month. 70% of students say it’s acceptable, at least in rare cases, to preempt an event by shouting down a speaker; 32% said the use of violence to prevent a speech is acceptable, at least in rare cases. Boise State has roughly 1.03 liberal students for every one conservative student. items.body: Here’s a not-so-bold prediction: It won’t take the State Board of Education a tortured 16 months to hire the next University of Idaho president. This next search almost has to go more smoothly than the last presidential search — the one that finally ended on July 1, when David Hahn took the reins at Boise State University . Smooth and transparent are two different things, however. And transparency is a thing of the past, due to a new state law that moves the presidential search process almost entirely out of public view. Retiring University of Idaho President C. Scott Green (U of I photo) " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/C.-Scott-Green-graduation-e1789667075837-1180x765.jpg" class="wp-image-125466 size-large" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/C.-Scott-Green-graduation-1180x787.jpg" alt="" width="1180" height="787" /> Retiring University of Idaho President C. Scott Green (U of I photo) So perhaps sometime next spring or thereabouts, the State Board will announce a successor to U of I President C. Scott Green , who announced his retirement last week. The vast majority of the Vandal family — students, parents, faculty and staff, alums and donors — will have only a vague idea of how the board reached its decision. They’ll never really know why the board made its pick, or who else wanted the job. In other words, expect lots of secrecy. What else can we expect this time around? Here are a few other predictions, based on the Boise State search. Expect a slower start . Actually, that’s happening already. In March 2025, Marlene Tromp put the State Board squarely on the clock. She abruptly accepted the University of Vermont presidency , in the middle of Boise State’s spring semester, with plans to leave at the end of the school year. The State Board announced its presidential search committee the day after Tromp accepted the Vermont job. The goal — perhaps unworkable from Day One — was to find Tromp’s replacement in time for the 2025-26 school year. Because Green is retiring, and not switching jobs, he is giving the State Board a lot longer runway. He will stay on at the U of I through June 30, the end of the academic year. That’s important, because college and university presidents often switch jobs in the summer. The State Board will be in no hurry to get the U of I job on the market for the summer hiring rush. At the front end, that gives the State Board a little more time to assemble a search committee and hire a search firm. It doesn’t mean the search will be more transparent. Just less pell-mell. The search committee could offer a big tipoff . The new law sets minimum requirements for the search committee: two State Board members, two university employees, two alumni, a foundation representative and a community representative. That’s all. (And no, students aren’t guaranteed a seat at the table.) There’s nothing stopping the State Board from naming more committee members. Or stacking an eight-member committee with a distinct emphasis. Regardless, watch the committee makeup. It matters, a lot. David Hahn, the sole finalist for the Boise State presidency, speaks to reporters in a Tuesday, June 16, 2026 press conference. items.body: Teachers and secondary students in the Nampa School District will get new MacBooks next year in a move to counter the rising cost of PCs as AI data companies gobble up the supply of computer parts. Nampa students have been using 11-inch HP Pro laptops that run on Windows, but trustees on Tuesday approved a four-year, $5.6 million lease agreement with Apple to switch to 13-inch MacBook Neos for students in grades 6-12. For years, Apple laptops have been more expensive than PCs. But Assistant Superintendent of Operations Cortney Stauffer told the school board that has changed. He said the switch to Apple will save an estimated $1.4 million over four years. Elementary students will continue to use iPads. Cortney Stauffer, executive director of operations for the Nampa School District " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-944x1180.jpg" class="wp-image-105832 size-thumbnail" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-160x200.jpg" alt="" width="160" height="200" srcset="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-160x200.jpg 160w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-496x620.jpg 496w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-944x1180.jpg 944w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-1229x1536.jpg 1229w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 160px) 100vw, 160px" /> Nampa Assistant Superintendent of Operations Cortney Stauffer “The PCs, believe it or not, are now significantly more expensive than an Apple Neo,” Stauffer said. Nampa’s switch to Apple comes months after the Boise School District made the same move. Boise trustees in July approved a five-year, $18 million lease agreement with Apple for 22,000 devices. “What we saw coming is a dramatic increase in prices,” Boise Director of People and Organization Services Will Goodman said. As EdNews reported in July , Idaho school districts face soaring PC prices as AI data centers buy up computer parts. Boise’s own Micron Technology, a large producer of computer memory and storage, announced in December that it made the “difficult decision” to exit the consumer market and sell only to AI companies to accommodate the “surge in demand” for data centers. Gordon Howard, director of technology for Bonneville School District, told EdNews that Micron’s exit is leading to higher costs for all sorts of technology. He said the cost of Chromebooks has increased by $100 over the past year, and the cost to buy new servers for the district increased from $6,000 to $10,000 within three months. “It’s not just Chromebooks,” Howard said. “It’s everything.” The resale value of Chromebooks is low compared to Apple products. Bonneville in July sold 1,488 Acer Chromebooks for $5 a piece. Howard said the district usually keeps Chromebooks for seven years, but that model of Acer Chromebooks became too expensive to maintain after just four years. Screens and keyboards were breaking. “It was just going to cost us too much to maintain them,” he said. “The breakthrough rate was just too high.” By switching to MacBooks, Nampa hopes to avoid that issue. The lease agreement includes 6,000 MacBook Neos for students and 650 MacBook Airs for teachers. At the end of the lease, the district will own the devices and can sell them back to Apple with a guaranteed buyback price of $120 for the Neos and $275 for the Airs. “This is actually a wonderful opportunity for the district,” Stauffer told trustees. Currently, students in Nampa are responsible for all damage to the PCs. Repair costs range from $50 to $120. Parents can purchase insurance for $25 a year to avoid those costs. items.body: Members of the Idaho Legislature's Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee and their staff tour Southwest Idaho Treatment Center, or SWITC, in Nampa on Nov. 20, 2024. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun) In January, as Idaho state lawmakers prepared for budget cuts, the state’s governor laid out a list of options for Medicaid decreases. One of them called to cut a set of programs that help people with disabilities live in their homes. In the end, lawmakers only adopted a more narrow cut to disability care. As federal protections fade, Americans with disabilities fear a return to institutions But as Idaho’s tight budget years dwell — and the federal government softens its stance on prioritizing keeping people with disabilities in their homes instead of in institutions — disability advocates are growing worried that home care might face cuts. Expanded decades ago, home and community-based services have become a staple for state Medicaid programs. But as the Trump administration seeks to reinterpret a U.S. Supreme Court decision that serves as a foundation for expanded rights of people with disabilities to receive care in their homes, disability advocates worry that home and community-based services could be threatened. Advocates maintain that the underlying laws requiring home care options remain. The federal government’s stance — detailed in a recent memo by the U.S. Justice Department — comes before states will see the impact of massive federal Medicaid cuts enacted in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. “When (states’) federal funding shrinks, they’re going to be reluctant to replace it with state funding, and so they will be tempted to try to reduce funding for home community-based services,” retired Idaho disability rights attorney Jim Baugh said. “But, I presume without a plan for what to do with the people who lose those services, or who have their services reduced, because we don’t have any alternative. So I just see this leaving people in the lurch. I see this being a dangerous possibility.” Several advocates also worry that there aren’t enough institutional settings to care for people with disabilities, if home and community-based services faced cuts. Earlier this year, Idaho officials estimated home and community-based services cost the state more than $176 million in state general funds, and were used by more than 16,000 Idahoans at least once a year. items.body: A mother holds hands with her son on a swing set. At least seven states have passed laws making equally shared parenting time the legal default in child custody cases. (Photo by Troy Bennett for Maine Morning Star) A growing number of states are making an equal split between parents the default child custody option in divorce cases. Louisiana and Mississippi this year joined at least five other states that have adopted the so-called 50-50 standard — four of them since 2021, as more legislators rework divorce-related laws that remained mostly unchanged for years. The 50-50 custody issue does not break down cleanly along partisan lines: The Mississippi bill was sponsored by Republicans, the Louisiana legislation by Democrats. Both states’ laws explicitly codify a custody guideline that many courts in other states follow. Supporters say a formal 50-50 custody standard makes divorce proceedings more equitable for fathers — who historically have been awarded less custody time than mothers — and encourages them to maintain an active role in their children’s lives. And it can reduce friction between separating parents by signaling they’re both starting the custody process on an equal playing field, said Don Hubin, board chair of the National Parents Organization, an advocacy group that has pushed for more states to adopt legal presumptions of shared parenting. Without that presumption, Hubin said, one or both parents may feel like they have to paint each other in a bad light in order to ‘win’ more time with their children. “It’s not just about the practice of shared parenting, but about the law signaling to parents that this is going to be the outcome unless something special is going on in your case,” he said. “It reduces the anxiety of the parents, which reduces the conflict between the parents.” But critics say the standard might harm vulnerable women and children by making it more likely that children must spend time with a parent who isn’t safe. They fear that for women in abusive marriages, the knowledge they would have to cede 50% of their child’s time to an unsafe parent could push them to remain in a marriage just to protect their children. Kimberly Rummage, who lives in Kentucky, calls her state’s 50-50 custody standard “absolutely diabolical.” She’s had a lengthy battle in court with her ex-husband over custody of their child. “I think that parents should have to prove why they get that 50-50,” she said. “You should have to show what you’ve done in that child’s life, what you know about that child, how you’ve participated and supported that child.” Some critics also argue that the 50-50 standard doesn’t account for the needs of children at different ages. Mississippi state Rep. Dana McLean, a Republican, warned her colleagues the state’s new law could harm breastfeeding infants who need to spend most of their time with their mothers during their first months of life. Mississippi’s new law requires family courts to use equally-shared parenting time as the default in custody cases. Parents seeking more time must present evidence showing why a 50-50 split isn’t in their child’s best interest. It also changes how child support is calculated: The new formula for 50-50 custody can lower child support payments for the parent with the lower income. Louisiana’s new law says child custody “shall” be divided equally, rather than “should,” which was the language under the previous law. In both states, as in others that have adopted the 50-50 standard, a judge can override the rule if the court finds credible evidence for awarding more time to one parent. But in Mississippi, several judges spoke against the bill before it passed, saying the old system — in which custody was awarded on a case-by-case basis using a specific set of factors — was the most fair. items.body: The Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee, the Idaho Legislature's powerful budget committee, meets daily during the legislative session. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho revenue exceeded the state’s forecast for the month of August by $37.5 million, marking the second consecutive month in the new fiscal year where revenue beat projections, according to a new state report. Through the first two months of fiscal year 2027, which began July 1, Idaho’s revenue collections have come in $51.2 million ahead of projections, according to the August edition of the fIscal year 2027 General Fund Budget Monitor. For the month of August, strong individual income tax collections that exceeded the monthly projection by $40.8 million helped push overall revenue collections ahead of forecast. Although it is still very early in the fiscal year, Idaho is projected to end the fiscal year June 30 with a positive ending balance of $657 million if state revenue collections come in as forecasted for the remainder of the fiscal year. That would leave the state with a surplus of more than $500 million compared to the budget state legislators set. Sen. Scott Grow, R-Eagle, makes a comment during the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting on Jan. 14, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “My reaction was its very promising report, and I’m glad to see the individual income tax is up,” said Sen. Scott Grow, a Republican from Eagle who serves as co-chairman of the Idaho Legislature’s Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee. So far, the state budget picture in fiscal year 2027 looks different than a year ago, when Gov. Brad Little and the Idaho Legislature implemented a series of near-across-the-board, permanent budget cuts to pay for a series of federal and state tax cuts and ensure a balanced budget, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Grow said the increased revenue, so far, in fiscal year 2027 is good news, but he isn’t in a rush to spend any additional revenue. Grow said the Idaho Legislature may have additional, unexpected expenses and bills this year related to Medicaid, wildfire suppression, health insurance costs for state employees and the state’s corrections system that may need to be addressed. items.body: (Boise) – As a state, Idaho is often described as self-reliant and independent. We take pride in local control, including when it comes to our public education system. Unlike some other states, we do not look to Washington D.C. to govern our local communities. We know what we need – and how to get it done. As the U.S. Department of Education continues its work to restore state control and localize educational governance nationwide, Idaho has put itself at the forefront of making the most of an opportunity to make our public system work for Idaho students – not for students in California or Washington D.C. This is a common-sense acknowledgement that different states and communities have needs that are best understood by the people who live and serve in them. The Idaho Department of Education has recently applied for – and was granted – a federal waiver that will allow the state to make its own decisions on the spending of certain federal dollars. This work was done in response to a general complaint that when states receive federal dollars for education, they have limited authority in how to use those funds to maximize student outcomes. Now, with this federal waiver, schools are better positioned to meet local needs. Idaho is now a proud member of states granted Ed Flex waiver status and is eager to make itself a leader when it comes to state-led improvements in K-12 public education. Simply put: the federal government gives schools a set of rules to follow. An Ed-Flex waiver gives a state permission to change some of those rules if there is a better way to help students learn. There is an additional waiver to be submitted later this month. The Returning Education to the States waiver is designed to provide flexibilities that honor the principle that the people who know their students best – parents, teachers, principals, schools, and states – should have more authority to make decisions that fit their needs. The waiver brings decision making closer to students, reduces unnecessary paperwork, and allows schools to use their federal resources in a way that works for them. These waivers, in addition to reducing state and federal testing for Idaho students, should send a clear message to Idahoans about where we stand when it comes to the importance of small government and local control. Idaho will continue to strengthen its reputation as a state where families feel confident in their public schools, where taxpayers feel assurance that their dollars are being well-handled and well-spent, and where students can work towards a successful future in their own communities and beyond. This is a major victory for Idaho’s kids and further reinforces that in this state, we value prudent, conservative stewardship of taxpayer dollars. The best answers for Idaho’s schools are found around kitchen tables, in local communities, and inside Idaho classrooms. By rolling back federal overreach, protecting parental rights, and honoring local leadership, we can build an education framework that reflects Idaho values, respects local taxpayers, and equips every child in our state to succeed.

items.body: The University of Idaho could get rid of its last standardized test requirement. If the change goes into effect for fall 2027, it would bring the U of I in line with other colleges and universities in the region, a university spokeswoman said Tuesday. The proposed change also comes in the midst of an evolving national debate over standardized tests. Most colleges and universities don’t require ACT or SAT scores, and some don’t look at them at all, but some of the nation’s most selective schools are reinstating testing requirements. For the vast majority of applicants, the U of I is already test-optional . High school graduates with a GPA of 3.0 or higher are admitted automatically, with no test required. The same goes for in-state students who score proficient of higher on the Idaho Standards Achievement Test. Graduates with GPAs of 2.3 to 2.59 don’t need to submit a test score either; they enroll through the Vandal Gateway Program for first-year general studies majors. The test requirement only applies to students that fall in a donut hole — with GPAs of 2.6 to 2.99. About 11% of the U of I’s incoming class falls within this range, spokeswoman Jodi Walker said. The U of I had dropped all testing requirements during the COVID-19 pandemic. Officials began looking at the U of I’s sole testing requirement in the spring, as this year’s application season drew to a close. This year’s numbers suggest the U of I’s recent enrollment surge is slowing — and probably for a number of reasons, including a shrinking population of 18- to 22-year-olds, and a rising public debate over the value of a four-year degree. University officials decided the testing requirement was one easy lever to pull, Walker said. “The landscape is changing,” she said. “Why put up barriers that don’t necessarily need to be there?” The decision, for now, falls to interim Provost Brooke Blevins . If Blevins signs onto the proposal, the admissions change would go into effect on an interim basis, kicking off a two-year faculty review. That would give the faculty time to see if the change is having an impact on enrollment and access, Walker said. Idaho colleges and universities set their own admissions guidelines — and Boise State University, Idaho State University and Lewis-Clark State College do not require SAT and ACT scores. Standardized test mandates have fallen out of favor nationally, and are rare in the West. According to the National Center for Fair & Open Testing (FairTest), a Brooklyn, N.Y.,-based group, only 7% of colleges and universities require standardized tests . The vast majority of colleges fall into a broad category of test-optional schools — and despite the U of I’s limited testing requirement for some students, FairTest lists the U of I as test-optional. According to FairTest, all colleges in Idaho and its neighboring states are test-optional or “test-free,” which means test scores aren’t even considered in the admissions process. But all eight Ivy League colleges and universities are reinstating their pre-COVID standardized testing requirements, and other top-ranking schools are following suit, Higher Ed Dive reported in August . The schools are facing some external pressure from the Trump administration, which favors standardized testing. FairTest Executive Director Harry Feder downplayed the trend. “Ivy Plus schools, as wealthy, exclusive national outliers, have increasingly gone back to requiring test scores for admission for their own institutional reasons and in response to external pressures,” he said in a recent news release. “The national picture of test-optional and test-free admissions is actually very stable.”

items.body: The Boise School District’s enrollment is down 699 students compared to last fall, according to a report presented to the school board Monday. The 3% dip isn’t a surprise. District leaders projected and planned for a 600-student decrease when they set their budget for the current school year. And it continues a trend that started about a decade ago. Since 2015, Boise’s enrollment has dropped 22%, from 28,078 to 21,805 this fall. On Monday, district administrator Jason Hutchison gave trustees two possible reasons for the downward curve: a declining birth rate and a lack of affordable housing in Boise. While Idaho’s population is growing, fewer residents are having children. Between 2005 and 2024, the birth rate among women ages 15-44 decreased from 78.9 per 1,000 to 58.6 per 1,000, according to the National Center for Health Statistics . The slowing birth rate means fewer students entering school, and that’s been a trend across Idaho’s public schools in recent years. Between the 2021-22 and 2025-26 school years, kindergarten enrollment statewide dipped 8.5% while 12th-grade enrollment increased 9.9%. In Boise, both elementary and secondary enrollments have decreased. But younger grades have decreased at a faster rate. This fall, Boise lost 428 elementary students compared to 271 secondary students. “Anytime your seniors are outpacing your incoming kindergarten class annually, which ours have been doing … you have a gap in enrollment,” Hutchison said. There are also students who were previously enrolled in the Boise School District but left for various reasons. Exit data shows that among the students who left the district during the 2024-25 school year: 57% transferred to another public school district or public charter school 17% moved to another state 8% transferred to a homeschool setting 7% transferred to a private school. Boise trustee Alejandro Necochea on Monday asked district administrators to share with the school board more information on the students who leave midyear. “How many kids are still in our community who just dropped out of our radar?” he said. Idaho Education News previously reported that the district cut funding for 17 jobs in anticipation of the enrollment decline. Assistant Superintendent Nick Smith said Monday that district administrators will continue to watch enrollment numbers before Nov. 1 — the cutoff for fall average daily attendance, which determines state funding for employee salaries and benefits. “We do anticipate that (enrollment) will fluctuate between now and Nov. 1,” Smith said, “so we do believe that 600 number that we budgeted on is going to be pretty realistic.”

items.body: The South Idaho Correctional Institution sign outside the facility in Kuna. The facility houses about 400 women and 300 men. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Correction: This story was corrected at 9 a.m., Sept. 16 to reflect that women state prison inmates are not sent out of state due to a shortage of beds. They are sent to county jails. If a woman incarcerated at the South Idaho Correctional Institution in Kuna has a dentist appointment, she has to walk through the men’s side of the prison to attend it. To do that, correctional staff must shut down much of the men’s side, restricting everybody’s movement to get her to her appointment. There are nearly 400 women and 300 men at the medium-security prison , which was originally designed for men. South Idaho Correctional Institution Warden Jennifer Tyvand (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) South Idaho Correctional Institution Warden Jennifer Tyvand is hoping a new women’s facility, slated to open in December 2027, will help solve many of the challenges of trying to house both men and women there. The new women’s prison is one of three new facilities the Idaho Department of Correction, or IDOC, plans to open within the next year. According to a preliminary budget request, the state agency will ask Idaho legislators in January for around $45.3 million to furnish and operate those new facilities to address a statewide shortage of prison beds. The new facilities will add nearly 1,000 new beds in the state prison system. The Legislature approved funding to build the facilities, but those appropriations didn’t include funding to furnish, equip and staff each of them. In 2022, lawmakers approved $112.4 million for a new women’s prison and $37.6 million for improvements to the medical annex at the Idaho State Correctional Institution in Kuna through House Bill 791. In 2024, the Legislature appropriated $10 million for the new facility in Orofino in HB 768. Bree Derrick (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Correction) “If we don’t open them, first of all, as a state we’d have nearly $200 million of investment that’s going to sit empty,” IDOC Director Bree Derrick said at an interview at the South Idaho Correctional Institution. “… In terms of the management of the population, we would continue to essentially limp along in the same way we have done, which means probably over-reliance on county jails and on out-of-state contract beds. And then, as it relates to the women, the women will remain here for the foreseeable future.” The state is short about 200 beds for women inmates, which means some are sent to county jails, according to the agency budget request. Idaho’s entire prison population is about 10,000 inmates, according to state data , but the total prison capacity sits at just over 8,200. The agency, along with all other state agencies, submitted its budget request to the governor’s budget staff at the Division of Financial Management earlier this month. In January, Gov. Brad Little will unveil his own state budget proposal, and legislators will decide how to appropriate funds during the 2027 legislative session. items.body: A quarterly report and an independent audit tell conflicting stories about the Idaho School Benefit Trust’s finances, according to public documents shared by the Idaho Department of Insurance last week. Meanwhile, included in those documents, internal board minutes show the trust painted a rosy picture of low rates and stability and unveil that the trust paid out $1.9 million on a single claim, shedding light on why some claims exceeded expectations this past year. The department is investigating what led to the trust’s collapse and has petitioned the court to take over and rehabilitate the self-funded health care plan that pays medical claims for thousands of public school employees and dependents. As of Tuesday, Fourth District Court Judge Lynn Norton has not yet approved the department’s request. “We understand that districts and other interested parties want answers now, and we ask for the opportunity to complete the examination and its determinations before drawing conclusions,” department spokesperson Julie Robinson wrote in a Monday email to EdNews. After receiving multiple records requests, the department last week posted 11 documents totaling 152 pages on its web page dedicated to sharing information about the trust. The documents include: Independent audits for fiscal years 2024 and 2025 One quarterly report the trust filed last year Three years of the trust’s internal board meeting minutes The department’s two civil filings submitted last month As a self-funded plan, the trust is required to submit unaudited quarterly statements and an annual audit to the department. The state then checks these documents to make sure the trust is complying with statute, including a requirement to keep a certain level of money saved up in surplus. Without enough money in the fund balance, the department has the authority to terminate a plan’s registration. The trust’s unaudited report for the quarter ending on May 31, 2025, shows it had plenty of money in reserves. It needed a minimum of $8.2 million in surplus and had $13.5 million, an excess of $5.3 million. After two years of losses totaling $7.3 million, the trust appeared to be having a good year. The report showed a net gain of $2.4 million for the first nine months of the 2024-25 benefit year, which began Sept. 1, 2024, and ended Aug. 31, 2025. Trustee and treasurer Darren Uranga, also CFO for Elevate Academy, signed the report on Aug. 5. But an independent audit of its finances three months later told a very different story: The trust was $11.3 million under the legal requirement to operate in Idaho. “It’s certainly something we’re investigating,” Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron told EdNews on Tuesday. items.title: We can’t stop Idaho from growing, but with more housing options, we can choose how
items.summary: In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening, writes guest columnist Ali Rabe. (Photo by Getty Images) Every week, public hearings across the Treasure Valley and beyond fill up with an emerging voice: residents, many of whom moved here in the last five to ten years, showing up to vote down
items.body: In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening, writes guest columnist Ali Rabe. (Photo by Getty Images) Every week, public hearings across the Treasure Valley and beyond fill up with an emerging voice: residents, many of whom moved here in the last five to ten years, showing up to vote down housing options their communities need. They organize, vote, and pressure local officials to reject more housing. I understand where that instinct comes from. I just don’t think it’s pointing us toward the right answer. Idaho leads the nation in housing growth. The data shows it’s still not enough. I grew up in Middleton, surrounded by farm fields. Those fields are gone now, replaced by one-acre lots with little infrastructure to support them. I’ve watched Idaho change in ways that make me sad, and I understand the anti-growth mindset. Too often growth here has meant sprawl, distant subdivisions, and longer commutes. But growth itself isn’t the enemy. Communities grow and change, and that change can make a place better, not worse. The Treasure Valley will keep growing. The question is how. During my nearly seven years leading Jesse Tree , the Treasure Valley’s eviction prevention nonprofit, I watched more and more Idahoans lose their footing here. People who worked full time couldn’t make rent, families were evicted, and some ended up homeless. In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening. Meanwhile, most of what gets built on our fringe is the same product: large-lot homes pushing half a million dollars, aimed at out-of-state buyers. Young Idahoans, our workforce, and longtime locals are left out. There’s a better path, and it isn’t new. It’s called missing middle housing, and it’s a return to how Idaho used to build. Missing middle housing means duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes, cottage courts, and small-lot homes woven into existing neighborhoods rather than dropped onto the fringe. It’s gentle, incremental density that adds homes without ruining a neighborhood’s character. Look at Idaho’s historic neighborhoods and you’ll find these home types everywhere. This is how our cities grew before exclusionary zoning took hold in the 1970s and made large-lot sprawl the only easy path for developers. It’s also better economics, for residents and for cities. Land is the single largest cost on a developer’s pro forma. When zoning only allows large-lot product, that cost gets baked into every home, which is why half-million-dollar houses keep getting built. Smaller homes on smaller lots bring that cost down and open the door to starter homes again. For cities, more homes per acre means more property value per acre without miles of new pipes, roads, and schools. It’s a better deal for taxpayers on both ends. None of this requires upending the neighborhoods people love. In my experience, when people see what missing middle housing actually is, rather than what they assume it is, most come around. Even hearing opponents soften once they realize it isn’t a five-story apartment complex next door. It’s a duplex that looks like the house beside it. I don’t fault anyone for wanting to protect what they love about this place. I love it too, farm fields and all. But protecting Idaho doesn’t mean freezing it in place, and it certainly doesn’t mean a housing market that only works for people who aren’t from here. It means asking a better question: how do we grow in a way that gives our young people, our workforce, and our own neighbors a shot at homeownership? Missing middle housing is one of the clearest answers we have. If you want to help make the case in your community, Gem State Housing Alliance is activating pro-housing voices across the state, and we’d love to welcome you. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

items.body: OpenAI is partnering with the Boise School District to give educators upgraded access to AI chatbot ChatGPT. The district plans to roll out “ChatGPT Edu” for its teachers in the spring semester. Boise joins more than 100 districts, charters and other K-12 organizations nationwide that have partnered with the company, according to OpenAI. The agreement gives Boise teachers and administrators upgraded access to ChatGPT while tightening data privacy protections. In an August interview with Idaho EdNews, Boise Chief Technology Officer Ryan Gravette called the arrangement “one of the strongest data privacy agreements” he has seen from a partner. Earlier this year, lawmakers had concerns about data privacy when they passed Senate Bill 1227 , which instructs the Idaho Department of Education to develop a statewide framework for integrating generative AI into classrooms. Some teachers already use ChatGPT, which harvests data from user interactions if they use the free version. Gravette — who previously worked at the Idaho Digital Learning Alliance, where he helped set up the same partnership — said he approached OpenAI to bring Boise into the program. He said teachers can use AI to reduce the time they spend doing clerical duties so they can focus on teaching students. “Wh at I think is important is that we’re taking a data-based approach around what really is the data showing,” Gravette said. “And let that guide the direction that the district is taking,” rather than the “emotional direction” of some community members. OpenAI sees an opportunity in schools Partnering with a massive tech company isn’t a first for Boise, Gravette said, adding that the district has agreements with Google, Microsoft and Apple. The OpenAI agreement involves no exchange of money, he said, though Boise purchased $5,000 in ChatGPT credits to allow users to exceed usage limits. Boise Human Resources Director Will Goodman, who formerly filled Gravette’s role, said OpenAI’s push to work with school districts reminds him of similar initiatives by Microsoft and Apple to get their software or hardware into schools at steep discounts. “T heir model was, ‘I f everybody grows up using an Apple product, they will buy an Apple product when they’re an adult,'” Goodman said. items.body: The Boise School District will pay $34,000 to a former student who twice encountered a transgender classmate in the girls’ bathroom last year. The district agreed to a settlement with Jane Doe — a pseudonym — after she filed a lawsuit arguing that the district violated Senate Bill 1100 . The law requires public school students to use bathrooms aligned with their birth sex, and it created a “private cause of action,” which gives students the right to sue a district that doesn’t comply with the law. Last year, the Boise district allowed transgender students to use their preferred bathrooms while SB 1100 was mired in court. After Doe twice encountered a transgender student in the girls’ bathroom at Boise High School, she filed a lawsuit seeking $5,000 for each incident. She also sought additional monetary damages along with attorney fees. The Idaho Family Policy Center (IFPC), a Christian, conservative lobbying group with a legal team that represented Doe, announced Tuesday that the district agreed to pay her $10,000 for the two bathroom encounters along with $24,000 in attorney fees. The settlement closes the first lawsuit brought under SB 1100. IFPC co-authored the bill. Republican state lawmakers enacted it in 2023. “The IFPC Legal Center is honored to secure a settlement for Jane Doe in this groundbreaking case,” IFPC Legal Center Director Caleb Pirc said in a news release. “Other Idaho public schools should take note that compliance with the law isn’t optional.” John Doe — a pseudonym for Jane Doe’s father — said in the news release that his daughter endured a “breach of her privacy.” “Not once but twice she encountered a male student in the female bathroom,” John Doe said in the release. “When she reported the incidents to school staff, she was told that it was their policy to allow males who identify as female to use the bathroom of their choice.” Attorneys for the Boise School District had asked an Ada County judge to dismiss Jane Doe’s lawsuit, arguing that SB 1100 was paused at the time of the bathroom encounters. In a separate case that wrapped up this year , the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals had issued a stay on SB 1100, pausing enforcement of the law between Oct. 26, 2023, and March 20, 2025. Doe encountered a transgender classmate in the girls’ bathroom in January and February of 2025. But Ada County District Judge Lynn Norton denied the district’s motion to dismiss the case. In July, Norton ordered that while the federal stay barred “enforcement” of SB 1100, it didn’t preclude Doe’s private cause of action. Norton allowed the case to proceed. It was scheduled for trial next year before the two parties agreed to a settlement. Dan Hollar, public affairs administrator for the Boise district, said Tuesday that the settlement “resolves disputed claims,” but the district “continues to maintain that it acted appropriately.” “Neither the District nor any of its employees admits, acknowledges, or concedes any fault, wrongdoing, liability, or other misconduct,” Hollar said by email. The specific terms of the settlement “are confidential and will not be disclosed or publicized,” Hollar added. “Out of respect for the privacy of the minor children involved, the District will have no further comment on this matter.”

items.body: An Alaska Airlines jet lands at Newark Liberty International Airport. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor) One of my earliest memories is sitting behind my dad in his airplane, pressing my face to the window, watching the big buildings shrink to look like Lego sets. I remember thinking: I want to fly a plane one day. The memories of flying with my dad – a fixed wing and helicopter pilot who repaired power lines – stayed with me for years of raising three wonderful children and working in sales. It wasn’t until my early 40s that I completed my private pilot license, the first step in my pilot career. I’m currently completing my instrument rating while working toward my commercial certificate, both needed to achieve my long-term goal of building a career in corporate aviation. My story matters now because women don’t need to wait until mid-life to become pilots. If the calling comes in childhood, follow it. Girls in Aviation Day returns to Boise on Saturday, Sept. 19, and I want as many people as possible, especially girls who may assume a cockpit isn’t for them, to see what’s possible. Women hold only about 5.5% to 6% of U.S. airline pilot jobs. This number has barely moved in decades, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Meanwhile, North American airlines expect to be 30,000 pilots short of what they need by 2032, despite the U.S. government projecting that there will be roughly 18,000 new airline and commercial pilot openings this decade. My timeline was unusual and now I’m training while balancing significant family responsibilities that don’t pause for flight lessons. Training is expensive, and self-funding my dream has meant real sacrifice for myself and my family. I’ve asked myself more than once whether it made sense to keep going. My answer has stayed the same: yes. I credit that to the mentorship I’ve received from other women in aviation. A scholarship through Women in Corporate Aviation last year helped me pass my instrument written exam and keep training toward my checkride. I pay it forward by mentoring girls through our local chapter of Women in Aviation and volunteering with events like Girls in Aviation Day, because I wouldn’t be here without seeing the many women before me who have made it to the rank of captain. Girls in Aviation Day brings around 250 girls ages 8 to 18 to Western Aircraft in Boise for a free day of aircraft tours, hands-on activities, and one-on-one time with women working across aviation and aerospace: pilots, engineers, mechanics, dispatchers, air traffic controllers. For many of these girls, it may be the first time they see someone who looks like them doing this job. Representation changes what a kid believes is possible for herself. While I didn’t have many women pilots to point to when I was younger, those in my life are instrumental in keeping me on my career path. I want the girls in the Treasure Valley community to have that now, not decades later. I want women considering aviation later in life, like I did, to know their timeline doesn’t have to look a certain way. Please bring the girls in your life to Western Aircraft at the Boise Airport between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. Registration is free at bit.ly/GIAD2026 . items.body: Idaho State Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield, a Republican running for another term in November, speaks to an attendee after a candidate forum on Aug. 4, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Sean Dolan/EdNews) This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Sept. 10, 2026. Debbie Critchfield wants $20 million to help school districts and charters keep pace with inflation, and support at-risk students. Even if the 2027 Legislature signs on, the $20 million would get carved up quickly. But the state superintendent said she prefers to enter the next session with a workable request, and not one that is immediately dismissed as “ridiculous.” “I’d rather ask for something that I believe we can get to,” Critchfield said Wednesday. After budget cuts, Idaho plans to maintain low government spending, state official says In an EdNews interview, Critchfield discussed the 2027-28 spending request she submitted a week ago — and the political calculus that went into her budget. All told, Critchfield is seeking more than $3.3 billion for K-12, a 3.9% increase. But her one new budget request is a $20 million slice of the pie. She wants this increase to go into “operational” spending — commonly called discretionary funds, because districts and charters can use this line item for any purpose. And that makes it a popular request in the K-12 community, Critchfield said Wednesday. So far, she said, she has heard only positive feedback from school administrators. “(It’s) the most flexible and customizable part of the budget for districts and charters.” However, there also would be a lot of pressure on the $20 million. Operational funding, now at $366 million, has essentially been frozen for three years. An increase could help address inflation. Schools could also use the increase to cover unexpected bills from the Idaho School Benefit Trust. Districts and charters are on the hook for much of the trust’s $13 million shortfall — and as EdNews reported this week, employee medical claims could be denied if a member of the trust refuses to pay their share of the $13 million. The trust shortfall came to light in July, but Critchfield’s budget has no money to address it directly. Lastly, the new operational money could support a rewrite of Idaho’s aging school funding formula. Idaho politicians have long discussed changes to the formula, adopted in 1994. Supporters of a rewrite, including Critchfield, want to provide extra funding to support at-risk students, such as special education students. While $20 million won’t cover a new formula entirely, it could provide first-year funding, Critchfield said Wednesday. Dedicated dollars could smooth the transition, covering schools that would lose money under a new formula. And this would be a departure from 2025, when lawmakers debated a funding formula bill that had no dollars attached to it. While Critchfield is pushing the $20 million line item, the Republican is seeking less money for the special education program she navigated through the 2026 Legislature. Her budget contains $1.7 million for a “high-needs” fund, for students who require full-time staff support or costly equipment. This year’s high-needs budget is $5 million. I t’s just so hard to think about how many people we lost.” After students read the names, former New York policeman Brian Bartley told his story. “A s we were sitting in a class lecture at police academy, my classmates and I heard the roar of a jet engine fly overhead,” Bartley recounted. “This was unusual as Manhattan is a no-fly zone.” He and his fellow rookies found it odd, but thought little of it.
