He never spoke publicly about his experience until around five years ago, when he started speaking at Elevate Academy’s 9/11 memorial. “It’s therapeutic,” he said. “ It definitely helps, and it’s more important that it helps remind people about what we’ve lost, what we went through, and teach the next generation so that they know why it’s important, why it’s not just a date on the calendar.” Here are some photos of Friday’s event: Click to view slideshow.

items.body: Wildfire smoke rolls over the skies near Warm Springs along U.S. Highway 26 on July 25, 2026. (Photo by Oregon Department of Transportation) Oregon lawmakers approved nearly $123 million to help cover the costs of this year’s wildfire season, sending money to two state agencies responsible for fighting wildfires. The Oregon Legislature’s Joint Emergency Board agreed to allocate $108 million to the Oregon Department of Forestry and $15 million to the Department of the State Fire Marshal at a morning meeting Thursday. The 20-member board has the authority to allocate funding when the full Legislature isn’t in session. As of late August, wildfires had scorched across 2.5 million acres and cost the state $236.2 million. Those costs are expected to reach $350 million by the end of the wildfire season — putting 2026 on track to surpass the state’s previous $318 million record when wildfires scorched 1.9 million acres in 2024. The forestry department has been able to pay for nearly $79 million of those costs with federal recovery funding, grants and other contributions. With the emergency board’s approval Thursday, the agency will also borrow $150 million from the Oregon State Treasury through three loans over the next three months to maintain solvency through the end of the year. The State Fire Marshal responded to 12 destructive wildfires this year that cost more than $50 million. The agency’s $15 million request will cover funding gaps needed to address those costs. The federal government is expected to reimburse Oregon for some of these costs, though that money can take years to arrive. The Federal Emergency Management Agency still owes Oregon about $92 million in fire management and public assistance grants from 2020. These are grants a state requests if they are facing a catastrophic emergency, and the federal government agrees to pay 75% of the costs. Typically they take about two to three years to be fully released to the states. This is not an unusual amount of money owed, nor is it unusual that it’s taking so long to be reimbursed, according to Joy Krawczyk, a spokesperson for the Oregon Department of Forestry. The slow pace of federal reimbursements frustrated lawmakers. “Through the course of today’s allocations, we’re going to be taking general fund dollars away from our schools, from healthcare, from housing, from public safety, while we’re waiting for reimbursement from the federal government,” said Rep. David Gomberg, D-Otis. Lawmakers on the emergency board thanked all the agencies who worked to put out the wildfires this summer. “It was predicted to be tough,” said Rep. Mark Owens, R-Crane. “We exceeded tough by many levels in that period of time. Without the coordination, the dedication of the state agencies, and I’ll say our Bureau of Land Management, the U.S. Forest Service, Rangeland Fire Protection Associations, rural fire districts and the volunteers that are out there, there’d have been towns and houses taken out.” Oregon Capital Chronicle senior reporter Alex Baumhardt contributed to this story. items.body: Before I was a legislator, I was, and still am, an Idaho mom. Like many parents, I want my children to have the opportunity to receive a good education, find meaningful work and, if they choose, build their lives here in Idaho. That is one reason I believe the conversation surrounding the proposed Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus should include education. America’s demand for reliable electricity is growing rapidly. Data centers, artificial intelligence, and advanced manufacturing are increasing that demand, and advanced nuclear energy could play an important role in meeting it. The Department of Energy recently selected Idaho as one of five states to explore hosting an NLIC. These campuses could include fuel fabrication, enrichment, used-fuel recycling and reprocessing, advanced reactors, power generation, and advanced manufacturing. DOE estimates a campus could attract up to $50 billion in private investment and create nearly 25,000 jobs. Those numbers should get the attention of everyone involved in Idaho education. If Idaho pursues this opportunity, we should also ask: How do we make sure Idaho students are prepared to fill those jobs? Not every career in nuclear energy requires a degree in nuclear engineering. An expanding industry needs engineers and scientists, but it also needs electricians, welders, technicians, mechanics, construction workers, cybersecurity professionals, project managers, and many other skilled employees. We already have pieces of that pipeline throughout Idaho. INL partners with Idaho universities, supports STEM education and internships, and helped establish Idaho State University’s Energy Systems Technology and Education Center. The Center for Advanced Energy Studies brings together INL, Idaho State University, University of Idaho, and Boise State University. College of Eastern Idaho also has partnerships creating pathways into energy careers. We should build on those efforts. That means exposing students to STEM and skilled-trade careers earlier, strengthening CTE and apprenticeship opportunities, and ensuring our community colleges and universities are aligned with the workforce Idaho will need. It also means helping students understand nuclear energy based on science and facts so they can make informed decisions about whether these careers are right for them. INL already projects more than 2,800 hires through fiscal year 2029, even before considering what an NLIC could add. For more than 70 years, Idaho has helped pioneer American nuclear technology. Our experience has taught us about innovation, but also about environmental stewardship, safeguards, and accountability. Those lessons are an asset as we consider what comes next. I want Idaho students to be able to graduate from an Idaho high school, learn a trade or earn a degree here, and then find a good-paying career without having to leave our state. Economic development and education policy cannot operate in separate lanes. If Idaho wants to lead the next generation of nuclear energy, we should prepare the next generation of Idahoans to lead it. That may be one of the greatest opportunities NLIC offers our state. Rep. Erin Bingham represents District 32B in the Idaho House of Representatives, serving Bonneville County. She serves on the House State Affairs, Commerce & Human Resources, and Environment, Energy & Technology committees.

After a two-hour drive from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, to this secluded spot in Somerset County, it was nice to stretch my legs and feel the sun on my face. I had nearly forgotten how windy it can be out here. My brain sort of went on autopilot as my body started to slowly move forward, past the education center and a small group of tourists milling around, and onto a black granite walkway. Every few steps, I’d glance at an engraving in the pathway — marking the time and location of a terrible event that preceded what I’d see when the walkway simply ends. Passing through two towering concrete walls, my eyes were focused on the overlook ahead. The expanse of fields of tall grasses, trees and flowers disappeared from view. I reached the end and stood in front of a waist-high glass window, marked with the phrase: “A common field one day. A field of honor forever.” I was back at the Flight 93 National Memorial. Forty innocent passengers and crew as well as four al-Qaida terrorists lost their lives there. It was peaceful now. The sound of birds, crickets and cicadas merged as the wind picked up again. items.body: Debbie Critchfield wants $20 million to help school districts and charters keep pace with inflation, and support at-risk students. Even if the 2027 Legislature signs on, the $20 million would get carved up quickly. But the state superintendent said she prefers to enter the next session with a workable request, and not one that is immediately dismissed as “ridiculous.” “I’d rather ask for something that I believe we can get to,” Critchfield said Wednesday. State Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield, a Republican running for another term in November, speaks to an attendee after a candidate forum on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 20206, in Boise. (Sean Dolan/EdNews) " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/IMG_0932-4-e1789069506928-1180x682.jpg" class="wp-image-123622 size-large" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/IMG_0932-4-1180x943.jpg" alt="" width="1180" height="943" /> State Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield, a Republican running for another term in November, speaks to an attendee after a candidate forum on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, in Boise. (Sean Dolan/EdNews) In an EdNews interview, Critchfield discussed the 2027-28 spending request she submitted a week ago — and the political calculus that went into her budget. All told, Critchfield is seeking more than $3.3 billion for K-12, a 3.9% increase. But her one new budget request is a $20 million slice of the pie. She wants this increase to go into “operational” spending — commonly called discretionary funds, because districts and charters can use this line item for any purpose. And that makes it a popular request in the K-12 community, Critchfield said Wednesday. So far, she said, she has heard only positive feedback from school administrators. “(It’s) the most flexible and customizable part of the budget for districts and charters.” However, there also would be a lot of pressure on the $20 million. Operational funding, now at $366 million, has essentially been frozen for three years. An increase could help address inflation. Schools could also use the increase to cover unexpected bills from the Idaho School Benefit Trust. Districts and charters are on the hook for much of the trust’s $13 million shortfall — and as EdNews reported this week, employee medical claims could be denied if a member of the trust refuses to pay their share of the $13 million. The trust shortfall came to light in July, but Critchfield’s budget has no money to address it directly. Lastly, the new operational money could support a rewrite of Idaho’s aging school funding formula. Idaho politicians have long discussed changes to the formula, adopted in 1994. Supporters of a rewrite, including Critchfield, want to provide extra funding to support at-risk students, such as special education students. While $20 million won’t cover a new formula entirely, it could provide first-year funding, Critchfield said Wednesday. Dedicated dollars could smooth the transition, covering schools that would lose money under a new formula. And this would be a departure from 2025, when lawmakers debated a funding formula bill that had no dollars attached to it. While Critchfield is pushing the $20 million line item, the Republican is seeking less money for the special education program she navigated through the 2026 Legislature. Her budget contains $1.7 million for a “high-needs” fund, for students who require full-time staff support or costly equipment. This year’s high-needs budget is $5 million. (Photo courtesy of the University of Idaho) This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Sept. 9, 2026. University of Idaho President C. Scott Green will retire on June 30. Addressing the campus community at his alma mater, Green recounted success stories from his seven-year tenure, including advances in enrollment, research and athletics. He also reflected on the challenges of leading the U of I through a global pandemic and in the aftermath of the November 2022 off-campus murders of four students. Flowers and candles left for a makeshift memorial sit near police tape at the site of a quadruple murder of four University of Idaho students on Jan. 3, 2023, in Moscow, Idaho. Green said he came back, in part, to bring some stability to the president’s office — a revolving door at the helm of a university established before Idaho’s statehood. During Wednesday’s speech, Green noted that his tenure marks the longest of any U of I president since Richard Gibb. Gibb was president while Green was a U of I undergrad. Green graduated in 1984. items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho state government agencies’ budget requests for the next fiscal year are now publicly available. The requests, which are online on the Division of Financial Management’s website , are for Idaho’s fiscal year 2028, which starts July 1, 2027. After ‘tight budget year,’ Idaho ends fiscal year with positive cash balance On the heels of a 2026 Idaho legislative session marked by budget cuts after years of state tax cuts, the requests outline the state’s strategy of continuing to operate state agencies and public programs with less funding, according to the governor’s budget chief, Lori Wolff. In a media briefing last week, Wolff told reporters that non-discretionary funding for Medicaid, state prisons and public schools is eating up most of a recent projection of increased revenue. “We were very tight on our bottom line before, so it doesn’t give us a whole lot of room,” Wolff told reporters. “That really quickly takes up most of the increase in our revenue,” she said. “So, our focus this year is going to be on keeping those budgets at where we set them last year.” In May, she wrote a memo to state agencies instructing them to only submit barebones budgets, and that the next budget year was not the time to start restoring budget cuts . The budget request for the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare — the state’s largest government agency that runs Medicaid and other public assistance programs — is the only budget plan that hasn’t been published yet, the governor’s spokesperson, Emily Callihan, said in a statement. She said officials expect to post the agency’s budget request Tuesday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The requests are one of the first major steps in the process to fund state government. In January, Idaho Gov. Brad Little typically releases his own proposed state budget. Then the Idaho Legislature, which meets during the first few months of the calendar year, considers budget requests by state agencies and the governor as lawmakers draft budget bills. In recent years, Idaho’s powerful budget-setting committee, the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee, has shifted to a different budgeting process that splits agency budgets into barebones funding and new spending. items.body: A 2023 aerial shot of the Materials and Fuel Complex at the Idaho National Laboratory's desert site. The complex contains several specialized labs where INL researches nuclear fuels. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho National Laboratory) One of the most critical issues facing Idaho is one that has received little attention but has profound consequences for the future of our state – the agreement that would make Idaho the dumping ground for a third of the radioactive waste generated in our country. It’s not surprising that Idahoans don’t know much about this issue. Gov. Brad Little, who is pursuing this agreement , and U.S. Sen. Jim Risch have said precious little or nothing about it, apparently wanting to keep it under the radar until they are safely re-elected in November. New nuclear campus deal would require Idaho to accept, store spent nuclear fuel, radioactive waste Congressman Mike Simpson applauded the agreement , saying it will bring jobs to his eastern Idaho district. “Idaho didn’t become the nation’s nuclear leader by being afraid of hard problems. It became the leader by being the state willing to do the difficult, careful work that others wouldn’t. That’s still the right instinct now,” he wrote. The Trump administration will choose three states to create what it calls a “Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus.” The other states in the running for this dubious honor besides Idaho are Utah, Tennessee, Louisiana and Oklahoma. The chosen states will each have to receive 33 percent of the radioactive waste generated by the other 47 states. The public did not know that Gov. Little agreed to be one of the states until the Department of Energy announced it in late July. The memorandum of understanding that Little signed in July without informing Idahoans said: “The host agreement shall provide for the acceptance of out-of-state used nuclear fuel, spent fuel, and high-level radioactive waste.” In its announcement, the Trump administration promised that the campus will boost manufacturing, create jobs, promote American energy independence, and attract other unnamed financial investments. Of course, we don’t know what this means since Little and our congressional delegation have not told us what’s in the fine print. Idaho’s long history with nuclear waste To put the importance of this issue in perspective, it is important to understand Idaho’s long and dark history with radioactive waste. Starting in the 1940s, the federal energy site in eastern Idaho, which is now called the Idaho National Laboratory, became the repository for much of the nation’s nuclear radioactive waste. The issue came to a head in the late 1970s when the press reported that the federal facility had regularly poured low-level radioactive liquid waste down an injection well above the Snake River Aquifer, which is the size of Lake Erie and provides much of the water for southern Idaho’s farmers and ranchers. There was also concern about other radioactive liquid waste being stored in containers buried above the aquifer. items.body: Most of the Kuna district’s schools are below capacity, some by hundreds. That’s despite Kuna’s rapid population growth, leaving the district with a disconnect between community growth and public school enrollment. Superintendent Marcus Myers laid out the district’s capacity and enrollment numbers in a presentation to trustees Tuesday night. Hubbard Elementary: 263 students in a building with a capacity of 400. Indian Creek Elementary: 238 students in a building with a capacity of 375. Fremont Middle School: 532 students in a building with a capacity of 750. Kuna Middle School: 726 students in a building with a capacity of 960. Enrollment has dropped by nearly 4% in the district since last school year, falling from 5,703 to 5,501. Yet in 2025, the U.S. Census Bureau named Kuna one of the fastest-growing cities in the nation. “Right now we do have some room, and we want our classrooms full for the sake of our kids and for the great opportunities that we afford to kids,” Myers told trustees. Some students are choosing alternatives to traditional public schools. About 2% of school-aged children within the district’s boundaries attend charters schools, Myers told Idaho Education News. Increasingly, parents have more options beyond traditional public schools. Valor Classical Academy, a charter school, opened its doors this year with around 450 students enrolled. Myers wants to have conversations with local families choosing charters to understand what influenced their decision. “It could have nothing to do with the Kuna School District,” he said. Myers told trustees he’s also working with the city to identify demographics of families moving into the area to learn how many have school-age children. He’s unsure when he will have the data. Kuna’s enrollment appears to reflect a statewide trend : Despite continued population growth across the state, overall K-12 enrollment is declining, particularly among elementary-age students. One factor is declining birth rates, which fell from over 16 per 1,000 residents in 2007 to under 12 per 1,000 residents in 2024, according to U.S. census data. Kuna has also seen its heaviest declines among elementary students. Some parents also cited homeschooling in a recent Kuna School District survey. Other families may be choosing private or charter schools, though it’s unclear how many students leaving public schools are taking advantage of Idaho’s $50 million Parental Choice Tax Credit. The Idaho State Tax Commission won’t release data showing how many recipients previously enrolled their children in public schools. items.body: Idaho’s colleges and universities hope to reverse a big budget cut from last year. The schools would use much of the money to bolster high-demand academic fields or cover the cost of growth. The budget request centers on a complicated line item that Gov. Brad Little refused to fund in 2026 — enrollment workload adjustment, or EWA. Using a three-year average of weighted credit hours, EWA is designed to provide additional money to growing colleges and universities. But with enrollment growing throughout the higher ed system, all eight of the state’s colleges and universities would stand to get some EWA funding. The EWA proposal: A breakdown The higher ed budget requests, submitted by the State Board of Education last week , come to more than $884 million. The EWA line item comes to a relatively small fraction, $12.1 million. Here’s where that money would go, and why the colleges and universities are pushing for a share: Boise State University: $5.3 million . Boise State would focus its money on high-demand programs in health professions, engineering and construction management. Some money would go into University Foundations, required undergraduate classes across all disciplines. “This support is vital to reduce student waitlists and faculty overloads, maintain accreditation, expand program capacity, and ensure students have access to required courses and high-quality instruction to ensure timely graduation,” according to Boise State’s request. About $2.2 million would go into personnel, including 18 faculty positions. University of Idaho: $2.6 million . The U of I plans to fund teaching assistant positions and student support through its Strategic Enrollment Management division. College of Western Idaho: $1.3 million . The money would go entirely into personnel, including five staff positions and nine instructors in high-demand fields. “(CWI) estimates that the student population will attempt over 145,000 credit hours in the 2026-27 academic year,” CWI said in its budget request. “This is 21% more than the 119,988 credits attempted in the 2023-2024 academic year, just three years ago.” College of Southern Idaho: $986,000 . items.body: A voter deposits a mail-in ballot at the drop box outside the Chester County Government Center in Pennsylvania on Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star) Across the country, state election officials are waiting to discover if federal courts will allow the Trump administration’s restrictions on mail-in voting to take effect. In Idaho, like many other states , election officials are nervous the changes might come too close to the 2026 midterm elections, which are less than two months away on Nov. 3. Why the rushed Postal Service plan for mail-in voting has states in a panic The changes — proposed in a new U.S. Postal Service rule that implements an executive order by President Donald Trump — would require federal review of the design of absentee ballots and impose new rules on the design of envelopes containing absentee ballots, among other things. “In the moment, the biggest concern … is just we’re so close to the election,” Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, the state’s top election official and an elected Republican, said in an interview last week. “There’s the practical implications of getting absentee ballots out.” McGrane said he isn’t sure that Idaho or other states would be able to fully comply with the USPS rule if it takes effect before this year’s election. He said county clerks across Idaho, who run the state’s elections, are busy finalizing ballots to print and mail out absentee ballots to military and overseas voters by Sept. 19. In Idaho’s largest county, Ada — which is home to Boise — election officials have told the state they need to know about any changes to ballots by Wednesday in order to make changes before they print the ballots, said Trent Tripple, the Republican elected county clerk for Ada County. He said he also worries about making big changes months before the election. “If you want the most secure election possible, do not put artificial timelines and make us change things at the last second,” he said in an interview. “If you’re doing that, I guarantee you there will be mistakes that are made — because we don’t have the time. We can’t back up an election.” And that’s all on top of other potential ballot changes facing Idaho election officials as the Idaho Supreme Court weighs a lawsuit by the organizers of Proposition 1, an abortion legalization ballot initiative, that challenges state officials’ descriptions of the initiative . (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The Idaho Supreme Court on Friday unanimously ruled that state officials must redraft explanations of the effect of voting for or against the proposed abortion rights initiative that will appear on voters’ Nov. 3 general election ballots. The court does not have the authority to write new language, but told the offices of the Idaho Attorney General and Secretary of State that they must submit revised ballot language to the court by 5 p.m. Saturday — around 24 hours after the decision was entered. Idaho Supreme Court Justice Gregory Moeller, right, asks a question during a hearing in this April 25, 2025, file photo. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The decision, written by Justice Gregory Moeller, found that neither the “yes” or “no” effect statements met the law’s requirements. “A statement is not ‘clear’ if it leaves voters uncertain about a principal legal consequence of their choice, and it does not describe ‘the effect’ of a vote if it materially misstates that consequence,” Moeller wrote. “Conciseness permits Respondents to omit unnecessary detail; it does not permit them to convey an inaccurate picture of the effect of a specific vote.” The ballot “effect statements,” required under state law to be a clear and concise explanation of the impacts of a yes or no vote, were written by Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and Secretary of State Phil McGrane. The state’s high court heard oral arguments Wednesday and issued a speedy ruling as election officials neared a Sept. 11 deadline to be able to send ballots to military and overseas voters. Supporters of the initiative, called Prop 1, filed a lawsuit on Aug. 27, arguing that the drafted effect statements of “yes” or “no” votes on the ballot measure were “misleading” and “confusing.” Attorneys representing Labrador and McGrane defended the statements in court, arguing they were the clearest and shortest way to inform voters. Joe Parris, a spokesperson for the secretary of state, said Friday the office is working to comply with the order. “We appreciate the Idaho Supreme Court’s prompt review of Proposition One yes-and-no effect statements,” Parris said in an email. “As directed by the court, we are working closely with the Attorney General’s Office to prepare and submit revised statements.
